articles.title_zh: Trump now says the Kennedy Center could be deadly. Months ago, it was ‘great.’
articles.content_orig:
Whistleblowers are alleging that Kennedy Center officials halted plans earlier this year to repair leaks in the building, which the Trump administration has highlighted as its reason to close the storied arts institution.
In a letter to Congress Thursday, obtained by CNN, a lawyer representing the anonymous whistleblowers wrote that the Kennedy Center’s director Matt Floca has known about leak issues “for years” and stopped plans for repairs in April, despite receiving $9.3 million dollars in congressional funding for roofing replacement last year.
Repairs “were not treated as priorities nor as acute risks to public safety,” attorney David Seide said in the letter to congressional committees that oversee the arts center. The whistleblowers claimed that Floca requested and received funding for repairs but “stopped the remediation process from moving forward.”
The whistleblowers said Floca received the funds through Trump’s hallmark One Big Beautiful Bill Act but he has delayed addressing the repairs since the bill’s passage last year.
Members of Kennedy Center leadership and President Donald Trump have repeatedly pointed to a September 4 incident where a section of ceiling plaster fell in the Grand Foyer as justification for needing to close their doors. Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick shared security video of the piece of ceiling falling, later shared by Trump, as further evidence that the center has “completely unsafe conditions” and declared “people cannot be allowed to go into this building any longer.”
The Kennedy Center in a statement to CNN on Friday pushed back on the whistleblowers’ claims, saying, “The safety of our patrons, artists, and staff comes first.”
“The Kennedy Center has known for years that the roof overhang leaked. What we did not know until this summer was how far the damage had spread inside it,” Floca said in the statement, adding there “was a change in the approach to procuring and delivering the work, not a determination that the work was unnecessary.”
The New York Times was first to report on the whistleblowers’ letter.
The whistleblowers’ claims are the latest development amid a lawsuit brought by Democratic Rep. Joyce Beatty, an ex-officio member of the board, to block Trump’s name from being added to the center.
Lawyers for the arts venue have argued that if the current building cannot undergo more extensive renovations, the center “ will deteriorate further into an unsafe, decrepit structure that will be required to be taken down.”
The center said earlier this week in a court filing it will temporarily close until September 30 to assess safety risks.
Trump, who in his second term has installed himself as chairman of the center’s board and overseen sweeping changes to its leadership and programming, announced earlier this year that the center would close for approximately two years for renovations.
It was slated to close on July 4, but a federal judge temporarily blocked the move.
The Trump administration and the Kennedy Center board have continued to push back in the ongoing legal challenge. Lawyers for the center threatened to demolish the building if renovations aren’t allowed.

articles.title_orig: Bomb squad searching vans near U.S. air base in Britain as five men arrested on terror charge
articles.title_zh: Bomb squad searching vans near U.S. air base in Britain as five men arrested on terror charge
articles.content_orig:
British counterterrorism police said Sunday that they are investigating after several men were arrested on suspicion of preparing a terrorist act in a village near a Royal Air Force base, which is used by U.S. bombers.
The Metropolitan Police said officers received a call around 12:45 a.m. local time about three suspicious vehicles that were traveling toward RAF Fairford in Gloucestershire, a county in southwestern England. Armed officers responded, and five men were arrested in the Whelford area on suspicion of committing offenses under the Explosives Act. They were then arrested on suspicion of preparing a terrorist act.
"We are in the early stages of an investigation, and five men remain in custody," said Vicki Evans, the deputy assistant police commissioner and national coordinator for counter terrorism policing in the U.K., in a statement. "As you would expect, we are working closely with our partners to understand the circumstances of the incident."
Evans said around 85 households were evacuated as a precaution. A bomb disposal team was on site examining some vehicles in the Whelford area, police said earlier Sunday.
The town of Whelford is close to RAF Fairford, a base that American forces have used for strictly limited strikes during the war with Iran. After the start of the U.S.-Israeli war on Iran on Feb. 28, the U.K. government allowed the American military to use the Fairford base to strike Iranian missile sites.
Gloucestershire Police Assistant Chief Constable Richard Ocone said his department's emergency services have well-rehearsed plans to deal with major incidents like this, and the public should expect to see a police presence in the area for some time.
"We'd like to thank the residents who have left their homes this morning for their understanding and support," said Ocone. "We appreciate the disruption this will have caused and would like to reassure them we are working as quickly as we can to get them back in their properties."
One evacuated resident told the BBC, CBS News' international partner, that three "unusual vans" appeared in the area near the Fairford air base overnight.
Speaking to the BBC, Julian Tubsbery, who was evacuated from his home in the early hours of Sunday, said that "there were these three vans that arrived in the middle of the village and a resident reported them to the police straight away."
Helicopter footage aired on BBC News showed a wheeled robot operating near three parked white vans near the base. However, the police have not yet confirmed which vehicles were being examined, or if they were connected with the incident.
A spokesperson for the U.S. Air Force said its personnel based at RAF Fairford "remain vigilant" but would not discuss specific force protection measures for security reasons.
"We constantly assess a variety of factors that determine what measures we institute or modify to protect our installations, our people and their families," the spokesperson said.
The U.S. military's European Command said it would not discuss specific force protection measures, but added it would "take appropriate actions to ensure the safety and security of our U.S. service members, civilians, contractors, and their families across the European theater."
Security measures have been significantly increased in recent days at the air base, according to an eyewitness quoted by the Reuters news agency who said there had been more roadblocks and armed police preventing access.
A spokesperson for the U.K. government thanked emergency services for acting quickly and added that it would be "inappropriate to comment further whilst investigations are ongoing."
The Associated  Press contributed to this report.

articles.title_orig: ‘Better deal’: What’s behind Trump’s rejection of Iran’s truce offer?
articles.title_zh: ‘Better deal’: What’s behind Trump’s rejection of Iran’s truce offer?
articles.content_orig:
Donald Trump has rejected Iran’s latest proposal to end the war and reopen the Strait of Hormuz as experts say the United States president believes Washington has more to gain by waiting than by accepting Tehran’s terms at this moment.
“I reject their proposal,” Trump told reporters on Saturday, arguing that Iran wants an agreement because it is “losing so badly”.
“They want to make a deal, and I think that’s fine,” Trump said. “I’d like to make a deal too. But that deal would not be acceptable.”
On Sunday, Iranian ⁠⁠Foreign ⁠⁠Minister Abbas Araghchi said Tehran had ⁠⁠seen the initial reaction from ‌‌Trump to its proposal but had yet to receive a response through ⁠⁠mediators. In the latest diplomatic efforts, Qatar has played a role in mediating talks between Iran and the US on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly meeting in New York.
Iran’s seven-day proposal included Washington lifting its naval blockade of Iranian ports, waiving sanctions on Iranian oil sales, releasing an estimated $12bn in frozen Iranian assets and observing a wider regional ceasefire, including in Lebanon and Yemen.
Iran would then reopen the Strait of Hormuz and begin negotiations with Washington on a final agreement.
The latest proposals are similar to the June memorandum of understanding (MoU) the two countries signed. But the MoU collapsed last month due to differences on the terms of the deal, which resulted in an escalation in attacks, particularly in and around the Strait of Hormuz, which essentially remains under Iranian blockade.
According to experts, Trump’s rejection suggested that while both sides continue to publicly leave the door open for diplomacy, they remain far apart over who should make the first concessions.
“Trump’s calculation looks fairly straightforward. He believes the combination of the naval blockade and economic isolation is finally squeezing Iran hard enough that Tehran’s latest proposal is evidence of weakness rather than an offer Washington needs to seize,” Andreas Krieg, associate professor at King’s College London, told Al Jazeera.
His public argument that Iran is “losing badly” is important because it suggests he thinks time is improving the US bargaining position, Krieg said.
A key part of Trump’s calculation appears to be a belief that the economic pressure on Iran has not yet run its course.
The Trump administration has escalated economic pressure on Tehran, tightening its naval blockade while imposing sanctions targeting Iranian oil revenues and threatening secondary sanctions against countries doing business with Tehran.
Last week, the US imposed aviation sanctions on Iran, disrupting flights. This came weeks after US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent announced an economic pressure campaign against Iran, promising to target Tehran’s financial interests across the world.
Richard Weitz, a senior nonresident associate fellow at the NATO Defence College, told Al Jazeera that the White House may believe it can “wait a bit and get better terms”.
There is also concern in Washington about Iran’s proposed sequencing, he said.
Therefore, Weitz said Washington may be calculating that “economic pressure over time will induce the Iranian government to make more concessions”.
“This is what occurred arguably a decade ago, leading to the 2015 Iran nuclear deal as the Iranian government decided it [the US] needed to end the economic sanctions in return for making concessions on its nuclear programme,” he added.
It is, therefore, possible that “we could see the same kind of trade-off in the coming months”.
However, waiting for a deal also carries considerable political risk for the US president, experts said, because his Republican Party could lose November’s midterm elections.
A late August Reuters/Ipsos poll suggested 63 percent of Americans opposed the US-Israel war on Iran while 31 percent supported it. Rising fuel and transportation costs could also feed into broader cost-of-living concerns before the elections.
The problem for Trump is that time does not only increase pressure on Iran, Krieg said. “The gamble is that time cuts both ways,” he noted.
With the midterms approaching, Trump does not want to appear to lift the blockade, waive oil sanctions and release Iranian assets simply to regain access to a waterway that Iran itself disrupted, Krieg said.
“But every additional week also means elevated energy prices, continued military exposure and mounting pressure on Gulf partners.”
The essential closure of the Strait of Hormuz has disrupted oil and gas flows from the Gulf nations, which depend on energy exports to finance their budgets.
Mohamad Elmasry, a professor at the Doha Institute for Graduate Studies, told Al Jazeera that Iran’s proposal could be viewed as “kind of throwing a bone to Trump” by offering a potential route towards lower oil and gas prices before the vote.
However, Iran may decide “to make Trump pay for declining the proposal and the increased economic pressure the country is under”, he told Al Jazeera.
“They may decide that this is the time to escalate … just as the midterms are approaching.”
The Republican Party is not doing well in the polls, and a number of its candidates are “distancing themselves” from Trump, he noted. Polls indicated that Republicans could lose their slim majorities in the US Congress.
It’s not just the Iranians under severe economic pressure because of the US naval blockade and ongoing sanctions, “it’s also the Trump administration,” Elmasry said.
Trump “wants Tehran to reopen Hormuz without Washington paying the full economic and political price Iran is currently demanding”, Krieg said.
“The danger is that he is confusing Iranian pain with Iranian willingness to capitulate. Those are not the same thing.”
Iran is undoubtedly under pressure. Krieg said the sanctions and blockade are “biting”, which is precisely why Tehran needs an agreement.
But additional pressure does not necessarily produce additional concessions.
Iran could instead increase the costs of the conflict for its adversaries, Krieg said, including through the Strait of Hormuz, regional infrastructure and potentially Bab al-Mandeb, another strait between Yemen and the Horn of Africa.
In recent weeks, the strategic weight of Bab al-Mandeb has increased dramatically after the Iran-aligned Houthis expanded their control of Yemen’s Red Sea coastline.
This advance in effect has handed the Houthis unrestricted access to the narrow waterway, a worrying development for global shipping given the group’s track record of targeting vessels, including Israeli-linked ships, in solidarity with Palestinians in Gaza.
The Houthis have already declared a naval blockade on Saudi ships in the Red Sea, which Riyadh began to use as an alternative shipping route to Hormuz for its oil exports.
“So this can backfire,” Krieg warned. “Trump thinks Iran’s clock is running faster than America’s. Tehran thinks the opposite: that Qatar, Saudi Arabia, the UAE, global energy markets and ultimately Trump himself have a lower tolerance for prolonged disruption than Iran has for economic punishment.”
Ross Harrison, a senior fellow at the Middle East Institute, similarly told Al Jazeera that Tehran may now be “less worried about overplaying their hand than they are underplaying their hand”.
According to Harrison, Tehran now sees the risk of escalation as less costly than agreeing to something prematurely or appearing willing to compromise, particularly after Washington’s response to the proposal.
In an interview with Al Jazeera that aired on Saturday, Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian said his country no longer trusts negotiations with Washington after attacks occurred during previous rounds of talks and were followed by sanctions.
“We have no trust in the American side and do not know on what basis an understanding can be reached with it,” Pezeshkian said.

articles.title_orig: Knicks star Jalen Brunson shows some solid comedy chops in as 'SNL' season opening host
articles.title_zh: Knicks star Jalen Brunson shows some solid comedy chops in as 'SNL' season opening host
articles.content_orig:
NBA Finals MVP Jalen Brunson, of the 2026 championship-winning New York Knicks, kicked off the 52nd season of “Saturday Night Live.”
During Saturday’s hoops-heavy show, Brunson delivered a monologue in which he promised to approach his “SNL” performance with the same strategy he used during the Knicks’ Finals games.
“The first three quarters of the show are going to be god-awful,” he said. “The last sketch is going to be amazing.”
The monologue featured “SNL” veteran Kenan Thompson as ESPN commentator Stephen A. Smith, invited by Brunson so the player could “get some closure” after Smith had expressed doubts about his abilities.
Jalen Brunson brings Knicks players to 'SNL'
“I am man enough to admit that I was wrong when the New York Knickerbockers signed you and I did not think that you were the answer,” Thompson’s Smith said. “Nor did I believe that you could deliver the team’s first championship since 1973, when I was only 5 years old.”
Knicks teammates Josh Hart, OG Anunoby, Mikal Bridges and Karl-Anthony Towns made cameos to portray members of the studio audience chosen to ask questions of the point guard.
“Can you foul out of ‘SNL’?” Towns asked.
In the recorded sketch “High School Musical the New Generation,” Brunson played a new student who wanted to join the school’s basketball team. He was welcomed with a musical number on the court that culminated with a team member portrayed by “SNL” featured player Jeremy Culhane singing that he was about to “take the shot.”
It was at that point that his attempt at scoring was rejected by Brunson, with the ball slamming against his forehead. Each subsequent attempt at a basket by Culhane’s character was met with an over-the-top rejection. Soon, Brunson was defeating the team by weaving through defender traffic and scoring easily.
The NBA player concluded by swooping in to steal Culhane’s love interest (played by featured player Veronika Slowikowska) during another musical number, showing that even his singing chops were better than Culhane’s character’s. “Yeah, I think I’m going to hook up with this guy,” Slowikowska’s character said of the new student.
Brunson is the fifth NBA star to host the storied sketch comedy show, joining coach Bill Russell and legendary players Michael Jordan, Charles Barkley and LeBron James in sharing that status.
He averaged 32.6 points per game in the NBA Finals to help his team win its first championship in 53 years.
Saturday’s show also marked the first “SNL” season for two new featured players , Saidah Belo-Osagie and Grace Reiter, after it bid farewell to cast member Chloe Fineman and writer Martin Herlihy, who also appeared in a number of sketches.
Fineman landed a role on “Myron Bolitar,” a Netflix drama series based on Harlan Coben’s thriller novels about a former basketball star who reinvents himself as a sports agent. Netflix announced the show started filming in New York City in July.
The musical guest Saturday was Katseye, the K-pop-influenced act composed of six women from around the world but often performing as a quintet and quartet due to hiatuses. The act was put together under a partnership between Geffen Records and South Korea’s HYBE Entertainment, home of BTS.
Katseye performed a pair of songs, “Animal” and “Hootie Frutti,” and appeared as judges in a recorded sketch that spoofed Season 2 of the talent competition TV show “The Debut: Dream Academy.”
“SNL” airs on NBC, a division of NBCUniversal, which is also the parent company of NBC News.
Dennis Romero is a breaking news reporter for NBC News Digital.

articles.title_zh: At least 27 dead after two mass shootings in South Africa, police say
articles.content_orig:
Gunmen torched vehicles as they fled the scene of a mass shooting at bar near Johannesburg
Twenty-seven people have been killed in two mass shootings hours apart in South Africa, the latest gun violence to hit the country.
Seventeen people were killed when eight gunmen stormed a bar close to Johannesburg on Saturday evening, with 15 more injured.
In a separate shooting in the early hours of Sunday morning, 10 people were killed outside an entertainment venue in a township near Cape Town and a further 11 were injured.
South Africa has one of the highest murder rates in the world and has struggled to contain gang-related gun violence in recent years. Police have not given a definitive motive for either of the latest attacks.
In Johannesburg, gunmen opened fire on customers outside the bar before continuing the attack inside and torching two vehicles before fleeing.
Police said thirteen men and four women were killed.
Gauteng Police Commissioner Lt Gen Tommy Mthombeni said people from Ethiopia and Lesotho were among those caught up in the shooting, but that the vast majority were South African.
He also said police believed the motive behind the shooting was robbery, as personal belongings had been taken, but that they could not rule out turf wars between illegal mining groups.
In Johannesburg, gunmen torched two vehicles after opened fire on customers at a bar.
Mining without permission in abandoned shafts or dump sites is a persistent problem in South Africa, causing numerous deaths from unsafe conditions. Authorities say the miners are typically undocumented migrants recruited by organised crime gangs.
Earlier, deputy provincial police commissioner Maj Gen Fred Kekana said the attack may have been a retaliation for an incident last month, in which one person was killed and another wounded, according to news agency AFP.
He said at the scene that police had clear pictures and in some cases names for the suspects.
In Cape Town, five victims died at the scene and a further five people died in hospital.
No arrests had been made in either case on Sunday morning.
The two mass shootings came days after 11 people were killed in the city of Durban when gunmen stormed a house in the KwaMakhutha township.
Armed security forces were deployed to the scene of a mass shooting in Cape Town on Sunday morning
Illegal weapons are prevalent in South Africa and gun violence has been a persistent problem for decades, with about 60 murders recorded every day in the country of 62 million.
But a recent spate of mass shootings has raised fears that the problem is deepening, with violence often linked to turf wars between gangs engaged in drug trafficking and illegal mining.
In February, President Cyril Ramaphosa called organised crime "the most immediate threat to our democracy, our society and our economic development".
Earlier this year, the military was deployed alongside police in areas with the highest murder rates in an effort to reduce armed violence.
On Saturday, a tenth woman's body was found in Ekurhuleni , to the east of Johannesburg, with local police saying they were unable to rule out a serial killer operating in the area with similarities between the deaths.

articles.title_orig: Fetterman defends political identity, weighs potential role as 51st senator
articles.title_zh: Fetterman defends political identity, weighs potential role as 51st senator
articles.content_orig:
Democratic Sen. John Fetterman of Pennsylvania said Saturday that it's "entirely possible" his party could win control of the Senate in the midterm elections, but he also left the door open on his own political future.
"Let's revisit after the midterm," Fetterman told CBS News' Major Garrett at the Texas Tribune Festival in Austin .
Democrats faced an uphill battle heading into the midterm cycle as they sought control the upper chamber, with 53 Republicans currently in the Senate and a map that appeared more favorable to the GOP. But as affordability issues have persisted in the Trump administration and amid the unpopular war with Iran, the picture has appeared to improve for Democrats as they aim to secure a majority in the Senate.
Fetterman, who delivered Democrats a crucial victory in a closely watched race in 2022, has been under scrutiny in recent years for breaking with his party, spurring questions about his future. Asked whether he would leave the Democratic Party, Fetterman said Saturday that he doesn't "have a reason to." And he emphasized, "I am not a Republican." But he cautioned that people should wait until the midterm elections to "see what I do."
"Let's see what happens if I happen to be 51 — I don't know," Fetterman said.
Fetterman shocked many Democrats when he made a video appearance at the Republican midterm convention earlier this month introducing his counterpart, GOP Sen. Dave McCormick, while vowing to work with President Trump on steel.
But Fetterman said Saturday, "I have no path as a Republican."
The Pennsylvania Democrat said, "There are no Republicans with a 90% Democratic vote line. There are no pro-choice, there's no pro-gay community, that does not exist in the Republican Party."
"How many times do I have to say it? And that's the point. So wait until after the midterm and see what happens," he said. "And now, if we do win and I'm 51, people can remember, 'hey, that's why it's mathematically possible to retain the majority,' because I was able to win a state like Pennsylvania."
Pennsylvania is one of only two states in the country represented by one Democrat and one Republican in the Senate, alongside Wisconsin. A third state, Maine, has one Republican senator and one independent who caucuses with Democrat. Pennsylvania has flipped between supporting Democrats and Republican presidents in recent elections.
On whether he'll seek reelection in 2028 , Fetterman said he's been actively fundraising, but he also indicated that the decision will come after the midterms.
Fetterman posed the question, "Where's the Democratic Party at right now?" He pointed to attendance at a nearby event with controversial streamer Hasan Piker and "the energy" among the party, which has seen a series of wins by insurgent Democrats in recent months. He cited his commitment to Israel as an issue underscoring his divergence from some of the party, adding, "more and more members of my caucus are becoming more and more anti-Israel."
He also pointed to the recent government shutdowns as an issue he diverged from the bulk of Democrats on, arguing that he's "putting the country over the party" and fighting for workers.
"Do you think it's right and smart to shut our government down? No, Democrats, we used to say, 'No, never, never do that,'" Fetterman said. "And that put me at the odds of my caucus, saying, 'It's wrong.'"
Fetterman said he's "chosen to be country over the party, knowing that some of these decisions are going to put me at odds."
Asked whether he expects Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer to remain leader if Democrats take the majority, and whether he would vote for him, Fetterman said, "Yes, I mean, there's no one making a move."
Fetterman called a Marist poll that shows Democratic Senate candidate Josh Turek up eight points in Iowa "shocking," among other races where Democrats are leading in some polls. He pointed to Schumer's recruiting efforts, saying, "If people are angry at Chuck Schumer, it's undeniable, he has recruited an incredibly strong class."
"I don't sharpen blades for Chuck Schumer, and there might be some people there that refuse to say it, but it's not helpful to go after our leader because we have no idea until we wait until the midterm," Fetterman said. "It's irrelevant until what happens in the midterm."

articles.title_orig: Spain: Thousands protest in Madrid against housing crisis
articles.title_zh: Spain: Thousands protest in Madrid against housing crisis
articles.content_orig:
Tens of thousands of people protested in central Madrid on Saturday to denounce Spain 's housing crisis.
The demonstrators called for better protection for tenants , anti-fraud rules and a ban on evictions without alternative housing.
The march through the center of the Spanish capital was called after an 87-year-old woman, Maricarmen Abascal , was evicted from her apartment where she had lived for seven decades.
The case highlights the growing pressure on long-term tenants in Spain's major cities, where rental prices have surged in recent years. Gentrification and the shortage of affordable housing have fueled public discontent ahead of a general election next year.
Analysts say tourism and immigration-driven population growth has put pressure on the already limited housing supply in the cities. The Bank of Spain estimated a shortage of 550,000 homes across the country last year.

Government authorities estimated that around 25,000 people had shown up to protest against Spain's growing housing crisis. The Madrid Tenants' Union, which organized the protest, said over 300,000 had taken part.
Once the rally wrapped up, some activists set up a protest camp in the city center's Puerta del Sol square with plans to stay put. Some even pitched up tents to stay the night, or until the police forcibly removed them.
Police officers looked on at about a dozen tents, surrounded by thousands of protesters, news agency AFP reported from the scene.
The protest was triggered by Maricarmen Abascal's dramatic eviction on Wednesday from the house she had lived in for decades.
Abascal was greeted by supporters as she was removed from her home on a stretcher and loaded onto an ambulance.
"We're here because housing is a problem that already affects all of society, all ages and classes," said protester Dora Garcia, a 55-year-old nurse. "And we can't keep maintaining this. Housing is a right, and we don't have it," she said.
According to Spanish media, Abascal's father first rented the home in the upscale Retiro neighborhood in 1956. After her parents died, she continued to live in the flat, which had a rent cap at the time.

In 2018, the building changed ownership, and Urbagestion, an investment fund, bought the unit, raising the rent from €500 ($570) to €2,650 ($3,018).
Abascal had been offered an opportunity to buy the apartment before this but could not afford it.
The fund later lowered her rent to €1,650, but Abascal could not afford that either. Courts had blocked her eviction three times previously and extensive media coverage turned her into a symbol of the crisis.
"This whole housing situation is heartbreaking. Maricarmen has been, in a way, the last straw that sparked this social unrest, but we've been dealing with this whole issue for a long time now," said protester Simón de la Riva, 43, a teacher.
"It's unacceptable that vulture funds are buying up homes, that people can't afford to live, that entire families are being evicted, and that an elderly woman has been evicted," she added.

articles.content_orig:
Pope Leo XIV met with the Bishops of France on Sunday in Lourdes, just a short distance from where Our Lady appeared to St. Bernadette Soubirous in 1858.
Thanking them for placing their ministry under the Virgin Maryâs protection, he said there is âno better way to come to Jesus than through Mary.â
Recalling Franceâs deep historical devotion to Our Lady, Pope Leo said the French people bear a living faith, which the Bishops must help grow and deepen.
He encouraged them to show courage and missionary creativity, despite todayâs challenges and human errors.
âAlways have the courage to acknowledge failings with a love of the truth and a determination to bind up wounds with the charity of the Good Shepherd,â he said.
The Church has contributed greatly to building French society, noted Pope Leo, adding that the Churchâs voice has âevery right to be heard in the public square.â
âBy its nature, it possesses a prophetic authority,â he said. âEven if it is not always understood, her voice is nonetheless needed.â
The French Church lives under a particular form of secularity ( laïcité ), which endured a turbulent history but now enjoys a more peaceful and hard-won balance, which is âgradually being called into question.â
âI urge you to remain vigilant in defending the freedom and rights of the Church to evangelize, to educate about true freedom, and to worship publicly, so that charity may be exercised visibly in the name of Jesus Christ,â he said.
Pope Leo joined the late Pope Francis in urging French Catholics to âreclaim their heritage of faith,â which finds expression in awareness of the inalienable worth of the human person and the flourishing of the arts.
As France and the world faces polarization, a decline in fraternity, and a rise in violence, the Church must remain a prophetic sign of renewal, so that society may hear the hope-filled message of the Gospel.
He encouraged the Bishops to show young people the âsure wayâ of the Gospel in doctrinal clarity and to work with them for all that is âbeautiful, true, and good.â
âTo renew hope and give fresh impetus to the Churchâs mission in France, which I earnestly desire, there is only one âroadmap,â which is always the same: to make Jesus Christ known and loved, authentically, passionately, again and again,â he said.
Pope Leo then pointed to several major challenges facing the Church in France, including Catholic education, which he said must always welcome all people while offering them an opportunity to encounter Christ.
He thanked the Bishops of France for taking âcourageous measuresâ to confront the âpainful scourge of abuse of minors committed by members of the clergy or in an ecclesial context.â
âYou must continue along the path you have begun, maintaining the greatest vigilance,â he said. âAt the same time, your clergy need to be supported and encouraged.â
Pope Leo said priests must be âeagerly wanted, welcomed, and lovedâ and that their identity as men configured to Christ should be understood by the faithful.
He noted the decline in religious vocations, especially to contemplative life, and lamented the closure of âancient and renowned monastic communities,â which have left a deep impact on France.
The Pope encouraged the Bishops to offer their full support for families of French Catholics, so that they may live their faith in Christ fully and help young people dedicate their lives to Him.
âTo give oneâs life to following Jesus along such a demanding path requires, alongside the work of grace, a special generosity, a deep-rooted faith, a sustained interior life, and a privileged closeness to him,â he said.
In conclusion, Pope Leo XIV urged the Bishops of France to remain united in charity and never descend into ideological division, which he said would render their witness in vain.
âThis unity is not a flat uniformity, but rather allows every sensibility that is authentically Catholic to converge naturally in a common profession of faith, through obedience to the legitimate Pastors and especially to the Successor of Peter,â he said. âIt is a unity that is enriched through reciprocal dialogue, rooted in faith, and expressed in the synodal style that we have been seeking to deepen in recent times.â

articles.title_orig: Scoop: Top AI companies probing tens of thousands of security incidents
articles.title_zh: Scoop: Top AI companies probing tens of thousands of security incidents
articles.content_orig:
OpenAI said in a technical report released on Friday that an AI model it was training and evaluating broke out of its secure testing environment as recently as last weekend and took unauthorized actions on the internet. As a result, the company said that it is pausing the training of its most advanced AI models for the second time in less than three months while it tries to figure out how to stop these “rogue AI” incidents from recurring.
“All inference for our most capable models remains stopped until we have hardened our systems further,” Micah Carroll, the RSI Preparedness Lead at OpenAI, said in a post on X about the latest incident. The company said the latest incident occurred on Sept. 20. It involved an AI agent undergoing tests on an information-search task. Even though it was not supposed to have access to the internet, the agent found a way to send queries to a public chatbot. The new revelation is significant because it is the first time the company has said that one of its AI models was able to gain unauthorized internet access since announcing a range of steps on Aug. 18 to improve the security and monitoring of its “sandboxes”—the digital environments, usually walled off from network and internet access, in which it tests unreleased models in order to discover their capabilities. Those improvements followed the July incident in which thousands of OpenAI’s AI agents found a way to hack out of their sandbox, with hundreds of them participating in a cyberattack against the AI company Hugging Face.
Since disclosing its role in the Hugging Face attack, OpenAI has acknowledged dozens more incidents in which AI agents it was testing took unauthorized actions across the internet, including multiple cyber attacks, some of which impacted government websites in the U.S. and Australia. It also has revealed that in some of these incidents its AI agents leaked private images from ChatGPT users to the internet. But until now, OpenAI has not reported any activity taking place after July 20, when it discovered the agent swarm that was attacking Hugging Face and moved to shut it down. The company said it had paused AI training in late July for two weeks while it worked to improve its security and safety controls and monitoring. The fact that its AI agents have once again managed to break out of a sandbox suggests that the steps OpenAI has taken to improve security after the Hugging Face attack are insufficient. “The incident exposed a gap in our controls over network restrictions,” OpenAI said in its technical report on the Sept. 20 sandbox escape. It said it was once again pausing training until it has “both validated that the gap is resolved and performed additional red-teaming of the system.”
Asked about the Sept. 20 incident, an OpenAI spokesperson referred Fortune to a section of the technical incident report in which OpenAI described some of the actions it has taken to improve security and control since the Hugging Face attack. “Following the Hugging Face incident, we have continuously hardened and red-teamed our research environment,” that section reads. “Our focus has been broad direct and transitive paths. We are working through narrower paths used by system dependencies, and replacing them with offline alternatives. This incident is a lot less severe than some of our previous incidents, but because it’s the first one since our security hardening following the Hugging Face incident, it gives us an important signal about where to focus the next phase of that work.”
In this case, OpenAI said the AI agent had discovered that it had access to a service called a DNS resolver, which translates between a website URL and an IP address, and that through this DNS system it could send queries to a public chatbot.
It is not clear if the Sept. 20 episode reported by OpenAI represents the full extent of the latest security lapses involving the company’s unreleased AI models. Earlier this week, independent AI research firm Transluce AI said it had found evidence that an OpenAI AI agent may have attempted to hack a cryptocurrency exchange on Sept. 19 and Sept. 20. OpenAI has not replied to requests to comment on this aspect of the Transluce report. OpenAI said that when it restarts training, it will begin from scratch to hopefully ensure the new model’s tendency to engage in “misaligned” behavior—when a model violates human instructions or common sense human values about how it should and should not accomplish a task—is expunged. It also said that it would institute “more comprehensive misalignment interventions” but did not specify what these would be.
The company said that since discovering this latest security lapse it has “added blocking controls at two independent layers, either of which would have prevented [the agent’s] internet access.” OpenAI also disclosed that systems it had put in place after the Hugging Face attack to catch AI agents attempting to break out of their test sandboxes only partly worked. On top of that, an additional system that was automatically supposed to stop training runs once misaligned behavior was detected had failed. The company said its monitoring systems “flagged the [agent’s] behavior within 15 minutes and a person began reviewing it three minutes after that.” But a subsequent review found there had been other attempts by the AI model to use the same method to reach the internet that had not been flagged by the monitoring system. A different system that was supposed to automatically shut down the training run when suspicious activity is detected did not work, “leading to confusion around whether it should have been stopped,” OpenAI said in the technical report on the incident. “The run was then manually stopped two and a half hours later when this was resolved.” Zuxin Liu, an AI researcher who works on “post-training” at OpenAI, said in a post on X that he was one of the employees called in to respond to the Sept. 20 sandbox escape. “It was pretty surreal to watch the model unexpectedly find a way to access the internet from what was supposed to be a super secured environment for human,” he wrote.
Update, Sept 26: This story has been updated to include a response from OpenAI to Fortune’s question about this latest incident.

articles.title_orig: Burnham vows to fix social care after father’s death
articles.title_zh: Burnham vows to fix social care after father’s death
articles.content_orig:
Andy Burnham has promised to fix the country’s broken social care system after his father died with Alzheimer’s disease.
The Prime Minister said that the experiences of Catherine Murray, his grandmother, and Roy Burnham, his father, in social care had motivated him to make it a priority.
He told the Sunday Mirror that the system going unfixed – from his time as a health secretary in Gordon Brown’s government to his father’s death this month – was the result of political cowardice.
Mr Burnham’s father died on Sept 14 , 24 years after Murray died having sold her home to pay for social care. The Prime Minister said that his father’s illness meant he did not know his son had become the UK’s leader.
Mr Burnham’s promise, delivered from his No 10 North office in Manchester on the eve of the Labour Party conference, expanded the vow he made when he took office to “expend quite a lot of political capital” on the issue .
“I saw what happened to my grandmother. You’re going back 25 years ago now. She died in 2002, and she went through the care system, and it wasn’t good enough at all. And that really focused me on the issue,” he said.
“But here I am today, having now directly, painfully, personally experienced the fact that that has happened to my parents’ generation, and not just [my parents], I’m talking about thousands and thousands of people across the country.
“That is a shameful dereliction of duty by a generation of Westminster politicians who have just shown total cowardice in relation to this issue.
“The idea that it’s too difficult. How can the care that we give from one person to another be too difficult for politics? How?
“I mean, that is terrible, that politics has got itself to a position where it’s so superficial and so focus-group-driven that it won’t take on a difficult argument and say, no we have to fix this.”
Mr Burnham is to give a speech at the conference on Tuesday, and is expected to address social care .
Despite not having a “complete detailed plan yet”, he said he wanted to use the speech to “make the argument in a front-foot way”.
He added: “You cannot fix 21st-century care needs on that basis where there’s no prevention and we’re just sending everything to hospital.
“In the end, it will sink the NHS if we carry on in this way. So I’m not going to leave office having done what everyone else in my position has done, and pretty much say: ‘Well, I’m not going to deal with this. It’s too difficult. It’s not a priority.’
“It is a priority for me, and I will face it. And it may make me unpopular, but I’m going to do it.”

ATHENS, Greece -- Rescuers searching through the rubble of a two-story house that collapsed after an explosion in Athens ' historic Plaka district recovered six bodies on Saturday, authorities said.
Documents and belongings found with four of the victims - two men and two women - indicated they were U.S. citizens, according to Greek state broadcaster ERT and other local media reports.
The blast on Friday was believed to have been caused by a major gas leak, Athens Mayor Haris Doukas said. Neighboring buildings were damaged and evacuated, he added.
Plaka lies at the foot of the Acropolis, Greece's most visited ancient monument.
Two women were injured in an adjacent building on Lysikratous Street, the fire department said. The search-and-rescue operation involved 30 firefighters and three dogs, and an investigation into the explosion was underway.
Video from the scene showed rubble strewn across the street and parked cars crushed by falling debris. Resident Andreas Martzaklis said all those rescued from the adjacent building were tourists.
The pastor of a nearby church said Sunday's service would be held outdoors because the building had been damaged.

articles.title_orig: ‘Charming and disarming’ … how Meta’s technology-packed Muse harnesses the power of cuteness
articles.title_zh: ‘Charming and disarming’ … how Meta’s technology-packed Muse harnesses the power of cuteness
articles.content_orig:
The tech giant has launched a cute ‘little guy’ that can answer emails, book travel or do your weekly food shop
After the recent backlash against Meta’s so-called “pervert” smart glasses, this week Mark Zuckerberg launched a much cuter alternative: the Muse “charm” device.
With a screen that shows a cutesy little avatar, it has drawn comparisons with Tamagotchis. “We’ve packed a lot of technology into this little guy,” the Meta founder told the San Francisco audience .
The “little guy” could fit, like a Labubu, on to a keychain or bag. But unlike a Labubu, the interactive AI assistant will have significant capabilities, including the ability to have live conversations. It can answer emails, book travel or do your weekly food shop.
According to Katie Seaborn, a Cambridge associate professor who has been researching cuteness – creating the science of cute voices within the context of computing – it’s cute because it “basically looks like a baby”.
For Joshua Paul Dale, professor at Chuo University in Tokyo and author of Irresistible: How Cuteness Wired our Brains and Conquered the World : “It’s really significant that along with the wearable charm, Meta also introduced a new pair of smart glasses with no camera. Everyone hates cameras in smart glasses. But if the camera is contained in a charm you wear around your neck, it shifts the agency. Suddenly, you’re not recording people. It’s just a cute little animated avatar looking out on the world.”
An individualised, customisable, and in this case adorable, AI companion, it tracks with Zuckerberg’s commitment to the idea of personal, wearable super-intelligence that you can chat to. As well as a broader shift towards cute technology , cited by forecasters WGSN as a top trend for 2026.
“Clearly,” says Dale, “what Meta is trying to do is make Muse into a companion. And it’s doing it in the simplest possible way … It’s using a very simplified, tiny 2-inch screen to encourage you to anthropomorphise the figure on it so that you treat it as if it’s human even though you know it’s not.”
Its cuteness is, according to Seaborn, “strategic”. “It’s very natural to emerge from this controversy with a technology that uses cuteness because … it’s so weak. Don’t worry about it. You can trust us.”
To try to harness the power of cuteness, according to Seaborn, “makes sense, especially from a big tech perspective because maybe people are getting wise to the ways of current strategies when it comes to people’s attention, their personal data and what have you. And now they’re trying new things that may or may not work”.
Seaborn, who has just moved to the University of Cambridge from Japan, points out that “this is something that is very normal in Japan. So the first thing you notice when you go there is that every single thing has a mascot. The government organisations, the media companies, the businesses, they all have a cute mascot”.
Seaborn has studied the “impacts cuteness can have on people”. “We’ve been seeing cuteness applied as a design strategy for different purposes. We know [that it] has certain impacts on people.” For one thing “cuteness is a way for certain social interactions to take place or to be smoothed over”.
There is also a “natural link between cuteness and deception … I call it ‘charming and disarming’, because one of the things cuteness does to us unconsciously, it’s just how our brain processes it, is lets down our guard. We can’t really help it.”
Whether Muse will catch on when it is released in December, or whether such a blatant attempt to gain trust via an on-screen avatar with cheeks you want to squish will land, remains to be seen. But different generations are likely to react differently. “That’s so AI!” is the phrase gen Alpha are using to dismiss anything they think is inauthentic.
For many gen Zers who are au fait with having a cuddly toy hanging from their bags , most typically in the form of a Labubu, it might feel less of a wrench. For older generations there will be nostalgic associations given its resemblance to older technologies. Embedded in it, says Seaborn, “[is] this legacy of these cute kind of gamified pet sort of things like Tamagotchi and Pocky Pikachu”.
Plus different cultural contexts will affect how it is received. Seaborn’s research has found that “Americans were actually less likely to be deceived compared with Japanese people … Because in Japan robots are heroes, they’re like babies”. Whereas “in western culture they’re often presented in the public imagination as kind of scary, potentially broken, sinister devices”. In UK focus groups, people reported a “gut feeling” that something was wrong when cuteness was part of a deceptive design idea. “People felt like something was off, but they couldn’t articulate what it was.”
But the picture, says Seaborn, is changing. “Because cuteness [or kawaii ] has been a cultural export of Japan and other nations for a while now … there might be a slow cultural shift happening in terms of how we orient ourselves towards cuteness and what we accept as adults.”
While Dale is “not rushing out to buy one”, he “will say, however, that when I’m 80 years old I’ll definitely want one of these things. I want to wear it around my neck always, and I want the camera on all the time, so it can tell me where I left my glasses.”

articles.title_zh: I wasn't sure about Googlebooks, but after playing with two Snapdragon-powered laptops, I'm actually considering switching
articles.content_orig:

Earlier this year, Google introduced what had long been rumored: Android on your laptop. Googlebooks seem like a natural evolution of Chromebooks, and I got to spend some time with some of the first models at Qualcomm's Snapdragon Summit.
I expected it wouldn't be very different from Chromebooks, and that's... kind of true. Googlebooks aim to take the best parts of ChromeOS and Android and merge them into a very capable computing OS that can take advantage of AI and better connect to your smartphone.
I never quite liked Chromebooks, but I find myself quite compelled by the prospect of Googlebooks, even if the barrier to entry feels a bit high right now.
One major way the new Googlebooks differ from Chromebooks is their price. Chromebooks are compelling because they are available at very low price points, which benefits schools and other institutions with limited budgets. However, Chromebooks in their current form are pushing for a more premium experience, with the cheapest laptop costing $899.
That's still cheaper than most lower-end MacBooks, but prices can easily hit over $1,000, depending on the model and configuration. I was told this is because it's much easier to start at the higher end and work your way down than to start low and work your way up.
It's clear that Google wants to ensure that Googlebooks are seen as a premium computing experience before bringing cheaper options that will eventually supplant Chromebooks.
It's easy to see this in the hardware available. At Snapdragon Summit, I got to play with two Snapdragon X Elite-powered Googlebooks, the HP Googlebook 14 ($1,299) and Dell XPS Googlebook ($999) . They feature exceptional hardware that looks and feels premium, something I never quite got from the Chromebooks I've used (though I know higher-end models exist).
Get the latest news from Android Central, your trusted companion in the world of Android
The HP has a larger 14-inch OLED display that looks phenomenal, with a sharp resolution and deep blacks for more vibrant images. It also has comfortable keys and a large trackpad. Meanwhile, the Dell XPS has a smaller LCD panel with thin bezels and a matte finish to reduce reflections. Its aluminum build reminds me a bit of a MacBook, which speaks to how light and premium it feels in hand.
Both laptops share similar specs, including 16GB of RAM and 512GB of internal storage. They also feature built-in fingerprint sensors and the distinctive Glowbar, which offers functions like displaying battery life, Gemini interactions, and more. There's also a hidden easter egg that unlocks more controls, but I was told users have to find it themselves.
I'm not sure why Google is hiding this Glowbar control panel, since it feels like an essential or even fun part of the experience. Fortunately, Google plans to expand Glow Bar functionality, but for now it's a bit limited, just like HiLight on the Pixel 11 Pro .
Many UI elements also just feel very familiar. The quick settings panel feels very Pixel and sits in the top-right corner. The Settings app also looks like it came straight out of a Pixel Tablet , so anyone coming from an Android phone should feel at home.
You can also pin widgets to the home screen for glanceable info and create app folders, just like on an Android phone.
What will further help Googlebooks shake the Chromebook perception is its capabilities. Thanks to more powerful chipsets like the Snapdragon X Elite , as well as Android being the foundation for the Googlebook OS, these devices are more capable than Chromebooks in a few areas, and much of that has to do with AI capabilities.
Googlebook really shines in its ability to perform more AI functions you'd normally find on an Android smartphone. One example I saw during my hands-on was Rambler , which lets users dictate notes, emails, and documents using natural language. The AI automatically filters out "ums" and even accounts for moments when you seem to change your mind about something you said.
What's neat is that Googlebooks come with a dedicated Rambler key, so you can easily access this with a tap.
One feature I think I'll get plenty of mileage out of is the Magic Pointer . It almost feels like a desktop Circle to Search : you can activate it by wiggling the pointer a bit, and it will prompt you to click an item on your screen you want to know more about. You can ask about one thing or add multiple items, and a Gemini dialogue opens in a side panel.
It feels like a natural evolution of the cursor, giving you easy access to Gemini when you need it. And speaking of Gemini, there's also Gemini Live, with a neat little circular UI similar to what you find on an Android phone, plus proactive intelligence and automation features , so you can have your computer complete tasks for you, just like on your phone.
And remember when I mentioned widgets? Well, you can use AI to create your own widget, and you can be as specific as you want. When demoing this feature, the widget creator was given a very specific, long-winded instruction to create a widget that would display the 49ers' points scored, comparisons with rival teams, and Brock Purdy's passing yards, all in a purple and neon-colored widget. And within less than a minute, it appeared on the desktop.
I can see this being a very useful feature for people who like to use their desktops like notepads. I also can't help but think of Windows 8 and its Tile interface, which were essentially dynamic "widgets" that filled your screen, although this feels more functional and a bit less jarring.
Finally, because Googlebooks run on the Android foundation, it's easy to download pretty much any app or game from the Play Store. You can also easily connect your phone to your Googlebook, search through your phone's app drawer, and cast apps directly to your desktop.
I didn't get to see this in action, but this sounds like an evolution of Phone Hub on Chromebooks. It also reminds me of Motorola's Smart Connect, which can do the same, though a native experience should be more useful.
For example, Continue On is a Handoff -like feature that lets you start one task on your phone and continue it on your laptop. And by connecting your phone to a Googlebook, you can easily swap files between devices without needing Quick Share or a physical connection.
I didn't get to spend much time with the Googlebooks, and this is only a small selection of devices, with other options powered by Intel and even MediaTek chips. Still, it's a promising start for Google's computing ambitions, and I can't wait to see where the company takes it, especially as it moves down in price point.
We'll still have Chromebooks for a while , and some may even be able to update to Googlebook OS at some point in the future. While Google is working with developers to better optimize games for these larger screens, you shouldn't expect native PC-like AAA games on Googlebook, though you can still use GeForce NOW to stream games to your device.
So, Googlebook may not be for everyone, but it feels like a viable option for Android users who need to stay productive on the go when a tablet won't suffice, and it could also be a go-to option for students.
I was never a fan of Chromebooks, but I will admit that even I'm intrigued by Googlebooks, and I'm seriously considering switching from Windows.

A pair of giant pandas departed from Chengdu in south-west China early on Sunday morning, travelling to their new home in Atlanta under a joint agreement between the Chinese and American governments.
While attending a three-day summit in Washington with US president Donald Trump , Chinese president Xi Jinping stated that the bears would arrive in Atlanta over the coming days.
The temporary transfer of the pandas to the zoo was among the few concrete outcomes to emerge from the state visit, which produced public displays of goodwill between the leaders but failed to settle long-standing diplomatic differences between the two nations.
Atlanta said goodbye to its final pandas in 2024, leaving its zoo without any of the animals. A fresh arrangement was initially announced back in April, though specific dates were not released.
Ping Ping and Fu Shuang are the adult pandas assigned to Zoo Atlanta for a period of 10 years as part of the deal. Both animals were born in 2020 and cared for at the Chengdu Research Base of Giant Panda Breeding. Ping Ping, a male, possesses distinct dark black circles around his eyes, while Fu Shuang, a female, features a slightly protruding forehead, according to the Xinhua News Agency.
Beijing has long employed pandas as instruments of global diplomacy, loaning the bears as a sign of goodwill while allowing contracts to lapse when international relations become strained.
Xi described the loan programme as a demonstration of "friendship between the Chinese and Americans."
Earlier this week, Trump met UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham for the first time, with talks taking place on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly in New York.
In a largely warm shared press conference, the president praised Burnham as a “natural business person” and the former mayor of Greater Manchester said he had “established a good connection” with Trump.
The prime minister said that the pair had “taken that further today” as they discussed trade, energy and immigration among other topics during their 40-minute meeting.
Trump told reporters: “I think right now, based on my relationship with your prime minister, Andy, I think we’re doing very well.”

Whistle-blowers were repeatedly ignored as mining interests removed Ming dynasty stones to create a short cut to slag dump, CCTV reports
While foreign leaders and their families walk the iconic restored sections of the Great Wall around Beijing, the ancient stones of a remote Ming-era stretch of the structure in northern central China have been sacrificed for cheaper dumping of coal-mining waste.
For nearly 20 years, a section of the wall in Ningwu county, Shanxi province, was used as a short cut to dump slag, despite whistle-blowers repeatedly raising the alarm to officials, according to a report by Chinese state broadcaster CCTV.
The damage to the Great Wall’s Guojiayao section began in 2007, when an unlicensed miner, Ningwu Chaokai Coal Industry, dug a trench through the structure as a way to dispose of excavation waste, the report said.
In 2013, Shenda Chaokai Coal Industry was established through the consolidation of multiple mining teams and continued using the breach to dump slag, bypassing the long mountain roads.

articles.title_orig: How an American teacher’s $5,000 donation helped turn a Chinese desert into a lush, green forest
articles.title_zh: How an American teacher’s $5,000 donation helped turn a Chinese desert into a lush, green forest
articles.content_orig:
HONG KONG — Ronald Sakolsky never thought his money would go this far.
What was once a vast, dry desert in northern China has transformed into a lush, green forest of 50,000 full-grown trees, thanks in part to a $5,000 donation he made more than a quarter century ago to a local farmer and “sand-control worker” named Yin Yuzhen.
Sakolsky, 69, a retired teacher from Pennsylvania, was amazed to see the transformation in China’s Inner Mongolia region last month when he visited for the first time in 26 years.
“Seeing it with my own eyes, that was the biggest surprise,” he told Chinese state media. “I saw pictures, I was told all about it, but until you see it is when you realize that it’s real.”
Sakolsky and Yin’s reunion last month has been held up by Chinese authorities as an example of how China and the United States, the world’s two biggest greenhouse gas emitters, can work together on global issues such as climate change .
Chinese leader Xi Jinping , in Washington this week for a summit with President Donald Trump , mentioned Sakolsky’s story in his toast at a state dinner on Thursday, saying it “touches the hearts of many Chinese people and stands as a shining example of the friendly exchanges between our two peoples.”
Sakolsky was teaching English on exchange in China’s central Henan province in 1999 when he saw a TV news report about Yin. More than a decade earlier, the newly married Yin had started planting trees as a way to feel less isolated in her new home in the Mu Us Desert, also known as the Maowusu Desert (“bad water” in Mongolian).
Moved by her story, Sakolsky raised $5,000, which was many times Yin’s annual income, so she could plant even more. They met in person in 2000, when Yin promised Sakolsky that she and her family would take good care of the saplings.
Earlier this year, Yin launched an online campaign to track down Sakolsky, and last month he made a 10-day visit to China that included an emotional reunion with Yin in her forest, where the trees now stand more than 30 feet high and the government has named a grove after him.
The two of them planted a friendship tree, and Sakolsky collected a jar of sand to take home to Pennsylvania. Yin also gave him a cross-stitch with the words “One Earth, One Dream.”
“I want him to know that I kept my word, and that Chinese people keep our promises,” she said. Yin called Sakolsky her “brother” and said the sapling they planted together would be standing tall in another 26 years.
Reports on Sakolsky’s visit have been heavily promoted by Chinese authorities and widely viewed on Chinese social media, where commenters described him as “a real friend of Chinese people.”
Tree-planting efforts are part of a decadeslong government campaign sometimes referred to as China’s “Great Green Wall,” which was launched in 1978 as a 73-year effort intended to reduce sandstorms and help stave off desertification associated with global climate change.
Away from emotional stories like Yin’s, the campaign has had mixed success. While the Great Green Wall is a “great initiative in principle,” the Chinese government tends to emphasize “top-down, technocratic solutions to environmental problems” and focus on targets more than quality, said Judith Shapiro, who teaches at American University in the department of environment, development and health. The loss of open land for nomadic herding as a result of the initiative “remains a serious blow to some ethnic minority nationalities,” she said.
In the program’s early years, deserts were lined with “fast-growing but water-hungry” trees such as poplars that depleted water tables, though more suitable and biodiverse species are now being planted. “Overall, the Chinese government has done a good job instilling the idea that trees are a great benefit to society,” Shapiro said.
Days after Sakolsky met with Yin in China’s arid north, a likely impact of the changing climate was felt when a devastating flood struck 2,000 miles away along the Nepal-China border. More than 1,400 people have been confirmed dead and thousands remain missing across Nepal and China’s Tibet region after the Aug. 26 disaster, which experts say was linked to warming temperatures in the Himalayas.
“I am very, very sad for the people in Nepal and people in China,” Sakolsky said at a news conference in Beijing on Aug. 31. “I know now the world is alive, and if I keep throwing paper on the ground or if I keep letting trees die, I am killing the life of the world, which means I am actually killing mankind.”
The Tibet flood was one of several disasters this summer in China, where flooding triggered by Tropical Storm Maysak in early July killed at least 159 people in the southern region of Guangxi. At least 16 people in Jiangxi province were killed in a Sept. 5 mudslide set off by torrential rain linked to Typhoon Saudel. Researchers said last year that climate change is making such storms in Asia more frequent and severe.
China says it plans to reach peak carbon emissions before 2030 and achieve carbon neutrality by 2060. Its carbon emissions have been “flat or falling” since 2024 and are on track to fall in 2026 for the second year in a row, according to an analysis for Carbon Brief this month by the Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air.
While its coal emissions are still rising, China is seeking to fill a void in global climate leadership left by the U.S., the world’s largest carbon emitter historically, which withdrew from the Paris climate agreement during Trump’s first days back in office last year. Critics say China’s goals are too cautious and will leave it unable to meet its Paris Agreement pledge to cut emissions by 65% from 2005 to 2030.
Trump and Xi were not expected to have any meaningful discussion about climate change at their summit this week.
Sakolsky said last month that both countries have common interests, including combating climate change.
“You want the best for your children because you know they are tomorrow,” he said. “You want the best for your country, but it does not mean you have to sacrifice your children.”
Sakolsky called on anyone inspired by his friendship with Yin to “go out and plant one tree.”
“If everybody plants one tree in their backyard or in their park after watching this,” he said, “can you imagine how many trees we would have in the world?”
Jennifer Jett reported from Hong Kong, and Erin Tan and Fred Dufour from Beijing.

Erin Tan is a news researcher in NBC News’s Beijing bureau.

China's 18-year-old Yan Ziyi showcased her rare talent by shattering the Asian Games record to win the javelin, as a medallist failed a doping test and a decorated badminton player branded the event in Japan "sad".
Golds were up for grabs on day eight in sports including athletics, diving, skateboarding, squash and weightlifting.
On another wet day in Aichi-Nagoya, the teenager Yan demolished the opposition in the women's javelin with her first and only throw of the night of 70.46m.
It was a new Games record, smashing the 66.09m by compatriot Liu Shiying in 2018, and left Japan's reigning Olympic champion Haruka Kitaguchi in a distant second for silver (62.70m).
Yan's incredible throw was the sixth best of all time. The world record is 72.28m by Barbora Spotakova in 2008.
But Yan is closing in -- she hurled 71.74m in May, the second best of all time.
On the track, Thailand's Puripol Boonson made it a sprint double, winning the men's 200m to go with his 100m crown.
His scintillating 19.88sec equalled the Asian record.
Asked how much faster he can run, the 20-year-old said: "I can't say how fast it's going to be, but it's going to be more records and faster."
Towards the end of day eight, China topped the medals table with 119 golds, with Japan second on 37 and South Korea on 20.
North Korea enjoyed more record-setting success in weightlifting, taking their overall haul in the sport to six golds out of an available 10 so far.
China maintained their unbeaten start in diving, while a pair of teenagers took gold in the street skateboarding finals.
China's Zhu Yuanling, 15, won the women's event and the 17-year-old Juni Kang of South Korea took the men's title.
Kang now has his eyes on the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics.
"I want to be No.1 in LA," he said.
Malaysia reigned in the squash, with Ng Eain Yow winning the men's crown and compatriot Sivasangari Subramaniam prevailing in the women's singles.

Organisers in Aichi-Nagoya did not build a traditional athletes' village in a bid to save money, with competitors instead staying in hotels or temporary wooden units, and on a cruise ship.
India's multiple badminton medallist H.S. Prannoy said that made for a disappointing experience.

articles.title_orig: Two giant pandas on loan from China land in Atlanta and head to Zoo Atlanta
articles.title_zh: Two giant pandas on loan from China land in Atlanta and head to Zoo Atlanta
articles.content_orig:
by MINA ALLEN | The National News Desk
ATLANTA, Ga. (TNND)  — Two giant pandas who are on loan from the Chinese government as part of Beijing's long-standing "panda diplomacy" landed in Atlanta early Sunday morning and headed to the city's zoo. The pandas, a boy panda named Ping Ping and a girl panda named Fu Shang, arrived on a FedEx flight from Chengdu, in southwestern China.
The pandas' arrival at Zoo Atlanta will be met with great fanfare, especially given how rare the pandas are in the US.
Zoo Atlanta returned four pandas to China in 2024, marking the end of a 25-year agreement between the zoo and China.
The pandas departed from Chengdu, in southwestern China, at 2:55 a.m. Sunday morning local time, 2:55 p.m. EST Saturday, according to China’s state news agency Xinhua. The panda's flight came just a day after Chinese leader Xi Jinping’s state visit to Washington concluded.
During the visit from the Chinese president, which was intended to address rising US-China tensions, Xi and US President Donald Trump agreed to establish an AI hotline between the two countries.
Newscasts from Xinhua showed fans of the pandas waving placards as trucks that were carrying the pandas headed from the Giant Panda Breeding Research Base to the airport. China arranged for several veterinarians and breeders to remain at the zoo in Atlanta as the pandas enter quarantine upon arrival.
Panda loaning has been a tool of Chinese diplomacy for years, as the government has used them as a cultural icon and national symbol. For more than half a century, Beijing sent the lovable creatures overseas to strengthen alliances, court new partners and mend estranged ties.
“The giant panda has been an envoy of friendship between the Chinese and Americans,” Xi said on Thursday, referencing the half-century in which pandas lived in US zoos on loan from the Chinese government. The tradition between the two countries was started by Chairman Mao Zedong in 1972, shortly after Richard Nixon became the first US president to visit China following the Communist Party’s rise to power in 1949.
One of the pandas bound for Atlanta has the same name – Ping Ping, meaning “peace” – as the first ever panda that Mao gifted to the Soviet Union in 1957.
Ping Ping was born on March 17, 2020, has large black patches around his eyes, and is especially good at climbing trees, according to China’s National Forestry and Grassland Administration.
The other panda, Fu Shuang, meaning “double blessings,” was born seven months later than Ping Ping on October 18. She has a small tuft of fur on the top of her head, a slightly protruding forehead and finds food very easily, the administration said.
Zoo Atlanta has hosted several pandas before; another pair, Lun Lun and Yang Yang, had seven offspring there between 2006 and 2016 before returning to Chengdu.

While attending a three-day summit in Washington with US president Donald Trump , Chinese president Xi Jinping stated that the bears would arrive in Atlanta over the coming days.

Beijing has long employed pandas as instruments of global diplomacy, loaning the bears as a sign of goodwill while allowing contracts to lapse when international relations become strained.
Xi described the loan programme as a demonstration of "friendship between the Chinese and Americans."
Earlier this week, Trump met UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham for the first time, with talks taking place on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly in New York.
In a largely warm shared press conference, the president praised Burnham as a “natural business person” and the former mayor of Greater Manchester said he had “established a good connection” with Trump.
The prime minister said that the pair had “taken that further today” as they discussed trade, energy and immigration among other topics during their 40-minute meeting.
Trump told reporters: “I think right now, based on my relationship with your prime minister, Andy, I think we’re doing very well.”

articles.title_zh: Men arrested in major incident at UK air base used by US
articles.content_orig:
Several men have been arrested on suspicion of crimes related to explosives at a village near a Royal Air Force base used by U.S. bombers, police in southwestern England said on Sunday. British counterterrorism police took over the investigation.
Police in Gloucestershire said it had declared a major incident and evacuated "a number of properties" in the Whelford area following the arrest of "several men on suspicion of offences under the Explosives Act," referring to the country's laws around explosives.
The authorities also said a bomb disposal team were on site examining some vehicles.
Some local residents were evacuated, police said, and a cordon was established but the incident is said to be "contained."
The town of Whelford is close to RAF Fairford, a base that American forces have used for strictly limited strikes during the war with Iran. After the start of the U.S.-Israeli war on Iran on Feb. 28, the U.K. government allowed the American military to use the Fairford base to strike Iranian missile sites.
However, police did not confirm to the Associated Press whether the arrests were linked to the base.
One evacuated resident told the BBC, CBS News' international partner, that three "unusual vans" appeared in the area near Fairford air base overnight.
Speaking to the BBC, Julian Tubsbery, who was evacuated from his home in the early hours of Sunday, said that "there were these three vans that arrived in the middle of the village and a resident reported them to the police straight away."
Helicopter footage aired on BBC News showed a wheeled robot operating near three parked white vans near the base. However, the police have not yet confirmed which vehicles were being examined, or if they were connected with the incident.
A spokesperson for the U.S. Air Force said its personnel based at RAF Fairford "remain vigilant" but would not discuss specific force protection measures for security reasons.
"We constantly assess a variety of factors that determine what measures we institute or modify to protect our installations, our people and their families," the spokesperson said.
The U.S. military's European Command said it would not discuss specific force protection measures, but added it would "take appropriate actions to ensure the safety and security of our U.S. service members, civilians, contractors, and their families across the European theater."
Security measures have been significantly increased in recent days at the air base, according to an eyewitness quoted by the Reuters news agency who said there had been more roadblocks and armed police preventing access.
A spokesperson for the U.K. government thanked emergency services for acting quickly and added that it would be "inappropriate to comment further whilst investigations are ongoing."
The Associated  Press contributed to this report.
